cultural.vision_reason: This is a woven strip-cloth gown (tobe/boubou) with embroidered geometric motifs; the museum's own description attributes the weaving style to Yoruba rather than Wolof, but such wide strip-woven robes are worn broadly across West Africa including by Wolof men, so it remains plausible for the claimed group. The category is also misfiled as painting-mss when it is clearly a garment.

physical.title: gown; tobe
physical.summary:
Gown (tobe, boubou, riga). [NB This cloth has been wrongly folded, and the photograph is incomprehensible. It should be turned 90 degrees, and folded along the centre in the other direction, in which case it would look (as it should) like Af1966,01.7. The following description assumes this correct layout.]
Gown (tobe, boubou, riga): oblong shaped body with broad sleeves flared towards the centre. Composed of 79 narrow strips about 4 ½ inches wide, uniformly woven from dark indigo-dyed handspun thread, which has been woven by the Yoruba with a variety of the checkered ‘guinea-fowl’ pattern (called ‘etu’ by the Yoruba) by running threads of white cotton (also hand-spun) regularly along both warp and weft. Each of the strips has three bands of alaari magenta silk regularly placed within the ‘etu’. A small pocket has been sewn to the front, and both front and back have been embroidered in white cotton. The embroidery is either by the Nupe or Hausa in the ‘eight knives’ (aska takwas) pattern, using chain and buttonhole eyelet stitch; there is a large spiral at the front and another on the back. The knives themselves are embroidered on top of extra pieces of cloth that have been cut to shape and couched down. The neck is stated to be lined with European white calico cotton which has been dyed blue locally. The open edges have all been hemmed by hand.
